title: Prototype, Object Pool and dependency injection
scopeHtml: Scope: copying objects, pooling expensive resources, and DI as the replacement for hidden singletons.

notes.title: Prototype: the idea
notes.html:
Prototype creates new objects by copying an existing one instead of building from scratch. Use it when construction is expensive (parsing, DB lookups, big graphs) or when you want many variations of a configured template.

+-------------------+
| Shape (interface) |
+-------------------+
| + copy(): Shape   |
+-------------------+
   ^           ^
 Circle     Rectangle   (each knows how to clone itself)

Worked example. A game spawns 5,000 enemy goblins. Building one loads a 3 MB mesh and parses stats in about 40 ms. 5,000 x 40 ms = 200 s. Load one prototype, share the immutable mesh, clone only the mutable state (position, hp): about 5 microseconds each, so about 25 ms total.

Industry examples. JavaScript prototypal inheritance, Spring prototype bean scope (new instance per request for the bean), Android Intent copy constructor (new Intent(other)), Object.clone(), ConcurrentHashMap copy constructors, document editors duplicating a styled shape.

Everyday analogy. Photocopying a filled-in form and editing the copy instead of re-writing every field.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying Prototype is just clone(). The pattern is the idea; clone() is a flawed Java mechanism.
  • Not saying when copying is cheaper than new (it often is not).

notes.title: Shallow vs deep copy, and why clone() is risky
notes.html:
A shallow copy duplicates the object but shares the objects it points to. A deep copy duplicates the whole graph. Mixing them up causes the classic bug: edit the copy, the original changes too.

class Report implements Cloneable {
    String name; List<String> rows = new ArrayList<>();
    @Override public Report clone() {
        try { return (Report) super.clone(); }          // SHALLOW: rows list is shared
        catch (CloneNotSupportedException e) { throw new AssertionError(e); }
    }
}
Report a = new Report(); Report b = a.clone();
b.rows.add("x");   // a.rows now also has "x"

Why Object.clone() is disliked (Effective Java, Item 13): it skips constructors, final fields cannot be reassigned, needs Cloneable marker with no method, and the Cloneable contract is vague. Prefer a copy constructor or copy factory.

// AFTER: explicit deep copy, no Cloneable
Report(Report other) { this.name = other.name; this.rows = new ArrayList<>(other.rows); }
Report copy() { return new Report(this); }

Kotlin variant: data class gives copy(), which is shallow; copy nested mutable collections yourself.

data class Report(val name: String, val rows: List<String>)
val b = a.copy(rows = a.rows + "x")   // immutable lists: sharing is safe

Other deep-copy routes: serialize and deserialize (slow, needs Serializable), a mapper such as JSON round trip (slow, loses types). Immutable objects need no deep copy at all.

Decision gravity. Use immutability for shared parts and copy only mutable parts. Easy to reverse; the risk is a latent aliasing bug found late.

Common interview traps.

  • Not knowing that ArrayList.clone() is shallow too (elements shared).
  • Using Java serialization for copying in a hot path (microseconds become milliseconds).

notes.title: Prototype in code: before and after, and when not to use it
notes.html:
// BEFORE: expensive rebuild every time
Enemy e = new Enemy(loadMesh("goblin.obj"), parseStats("goblin.json")); // 40 ms

// AFTER: registry of prototypes
class EnemyRegistry {
    private final Map<String, Enemy> protos = new HashMap<>();
    void register(String key, Enemy e) { protos.put(key, e); }
    Enemy spawn(String key) { return protos.get(key).copy(); }     // cheap
}
class Enemy {
    private final Mesh mesh;          // immutable, shared
    private int hp; private Vec pos;  // mutable, copied
    Enemy(Mesh m, int hp, Vec pos) { this.mesh = m; this.hp = hp; this.pos = pos; }
    Enemy copy() { return new Enemy(mesh, hp, new Vec(pos.x, pos.y)); }
}

When NOT to use it. If new is cheap, copying adds only complexity. Skip it when objects are mostly immutable (just share them), when the graph has cycles or external resources (sockets, file handles cannot be cloned), or when you would rely on Cloneable. A factory or Builder is clearer in most business code.

Decision gravity. Alternatives: factory, Builder, flyweight (share the heavy immutable part). Breaks on aliasing bugs and on objects holding unique identity (IDs, locks). Reversible, but a missed deep copy is a data-corruption bug.

Common interview traps.

  • Cloning an object that has a unique ID, producing two entities with the same ID.
  • Copying a lock or connection.

notes.title: Object Pool: the idea
notes.html:
Object Pool keeps a set of ready-made, reusable objects and lends them out instead of creating and destroying them each time. Worth it when creation is costly (a DB connection takes tens of ms and a TCP plus TLS handshake) or when objects are scarce (connections, threads, GPU buffers).

Life cycle: borrow() -> use -> release() back. Fixed maximum size gives natural back-pressure.

+-------------------+      +-----------------+
| Pool<T>           |----->| T (reusable)    |
+-------------------+      +-----------------+
| - idle: Queue<T>  |
| - maxSize         |
| + borrow(timeout) |
| + release(T)      |
+-------------------+

Worked example. Postgres connection cost about 20 to 50 ms to open and about 10 MB RAM server-side. At 800 requests/s, opening per request = 16 to 40 s of connect time per second. A pool of 20 connections serves the same load with near-zero setup. HikariCP defaults: maximumPoolSize=10, connectionTimeout=30000 ms, maxLifetime=1800000 ms; a common rule of thumb is pool size around cores * 2 + effective disk spindles, so smaller than people expect. Postgres itself degrades past a few hundred connections, which is why PgBouncer exists.

Industry examples. HikariCP, Apache DBCP, ThreadPoolExecutor, OkHttp ConnectionPool (default 5 idle connections, 5 minutes keep-alive), Android Pools.SynchronizedPool for MotionEvent and Message.obtain(), Netty PooledByteBufAllocator.

Everyday analogy. A library lending books: a limited number, you return them, the next person borrows the same copy.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting release() in a finally block: a leak that drains the pool and hangs the app.
  • Not bounding the pool: it becomes a memory leak.

notes.title: Object Pool in code: before and after
notes.html:
// BEFORE: new connection per request
Connection c = DriverManager.getConnection(url);   // 30 ms each
try { run(c); } finally { c.close(); }

// AFTER: thread-safe bounded pool
class Pool<T> {
    private final BlockingQueue<T> idle;
    Pool(int size, Supplier<T> factory) {
        idle = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(size);
        for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) idle.add(factory.get());
    }
    T borrow(long ms) throws InterruptedException {
        T t = idle.poll(ms, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
        if (t == null) throw new IllegalStateException("pool exhausted");
        return t;
    }
    void release(T t) { idle.offer(t); }
}
// usage
T c = pool.borrow(500);
try { run(c); } finally { pool.release(c); }

Kotlin variant:

class Pool<T>(size: Int, factory: () -> T) {
    private val idle = ArrayBlockingQueue<T>(size).apply { repeat(size) { add(factory()) } }
    fun <R> use(timeoutMs: Long, block: (T) -> R): R {
        val t = idle.poll(timeoutMs, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) ?: error("pool exhausted")
        try { return block(t) } finally { idle.offer(t) }   // always returned
    }
}

The Kotlin use-style function makes forgetting release impossible.

Production symptoms: pool exhausted or Connection is not available, request timed out after 30000ms errors, rising wait time metric, active == max with idle 0. Causes: leaked connections, slow queries holding them, pool smaller than concurrency.

Decision gravity. Chosen to amortize creation cost and cap resource use. Alternatives: create on demand, thread-local objects, a library pool. Must reset object state on release (otherwise state leaks between users). Breaks when objects go stale (closed by server): validate on borrow or use maxLifetime. Reversible.

Common interview traps.

  • Not resetting state (a dirty StringBuilder or open transaction handed to the next caller).
  • Writing your own pool in production instead of HikariCP; in an interview, write it only to show understanding.
  • Sizing the pool larger than the database can handle.

notes.title: When NOT to use Object Pool
notes.html:
Do not pool cheap objects. The JVM allocates short-lived objects very quickly and young-generation GC is nearly free; a pool adds locking and risks bugs. Pooling Strings or small DTOs often makes things slower and keeps garbage alive longer (promoted to old gen).

Pool only when: creation is expensive (I/O, handshake), the resource is limited (connections, file handles, threads), or you must avoid GC pauses on a hot path (Netty buffers, Android Message).

Industry examples. Netty pools direct buffers because allocation from the OS is slow; Android pools Message to avoid GC jank on the UI thread; nobody pools Integer.

Everyday analogy. Reusing a coffee cup is sensible; reusing a paper napkin is not worth the washing.

Common interview traps.

  • Pooling to "improve performance" without a measurement.
  • Forgetting thread safety of the pool's own data structure.

notes.title: Dependency injection as a pattern
notes.html:
Dependency injection (DI) means an object receives the things it needs from outside instead of creating or looking them up itself. It is the cure for the Singleton and new problems: construction moves out of the class.

Three forms: constructor injection (preferred: object is valid when built, fields can be final), setter/property injection (optional deps), interface/method injection (rare). The composition root is the one place (main, Application class) that wires everything together.

+----------------+      +---------------+       +----------------+
| OrderService   |----->| PaymentGateway|<------| StripeGateway  |
+----------------+      | (interface)   |<------| FakeGateway    |
| ctor(gateway)  |      +---------------+       +----------------+
// BEFORE: class creates its own collaborator, untestable
class OrderService {
    private final PaymentGateway gw = new StripeGateway("sk_live_...");
    void place(Order o) { gw.charge(o); }
}

// AFTER: constructor injection
class OrderService {
    private final PaymentGateway gw;
    OrderService(PaymentGateway gw) { this.gw = gw; }
    void place(Order o) { gw.charge(o); }
}
// production wiring (composition root)
new OrderService(new StripeGateway(System.getenv("STRIPE_KEY")));
// test
new OrderService(o -> { /* record call */ });

Kotlin variant: class OrderService(private val gw: PaymentGateway); with Hilt, @Inject constructor(private val gw: PaymentGateway) and a @Binds module chooses the implementation.

DI containers (Spring, Dagger/Hilt, Guice, Koin) automate wiring and manage scopes (singleton, per request, per activity). Dagger generates code at compile time (fast start, errors early); Spring uses reflection at start-up (flexible, slower start, errors at runtime).

Decision gravity. Chosen for testability and replaceable parts. Alternatives: Service Locator (hidden dependencies, same flaws as Singleton), static singletons, plain manual DI. For interviews, manual constructor injection is enough; mention a container as an option. Moving to a container later is easy if you always used constructors: reversible.

Industry examples. Spring Framework, Google Guice and Dagger, Android Hilt, Kotlin Koin, ASP.NET Core built-in DI.

Everyday analogy. A chef is handed ingredients by the kitchen porter instead of going shopping for each dish.

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing DI (a technique) with a DI container (a tool).
  • A constructor with 9 injected dependencies: a sign the class does too much, not a reason to switch to field injection.
  • Service Locator (Container.get(X.class) inside methods) is not DI; it hides dependencies.

notes.title: When NOT to use DI (and how the patterns connect)
notes.html:
Do not inject trivial, stable things. String, List, value objects and pure functions do not need an interface plus binding. Do not create an interface for every class "for DI".

Connections:

  • Singleton becomes a container scope: one instance, no static access.
  • Factory is injected where the concrete type is chosen at runtime (a Provider<T> or Supplier<T>).
  • Builder objects are created at the composition root; the finished immutable object is injected.
  • Pool is injected as DataSource, never created inside a DAO.

Worked example. A service needs a different Notifier per request (sms or email). Inject NotifierFactory (a Factory), not a single Notifier, so each request picks the right one; the factory itself is a singleton in the container.

Industry examples. Spring ObjectProvider<T>, Dagger Provider<T> and @AssistedInject, Hilt @Singleton.

Everyday analogy. A power strip: plug in whichever appliance you need; it does not need a special socket per appliance, but you also do not wire a strip for a single lamp.

Common interview traps.

  • Over-abstracting: 40 interfaces for 40 classes with one implementation each.
  • Injecting a container into a class (service locator through the back door).

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Prototype: copy a configured object instead of rebuilding; beware shallow vs deep copy. Prefer copy constructors or Kotlin copy() over Cloneable; share immutable parts.
  • Object Pool: reuse expensive or scarce objects (connections, threads, buffers) with a bounded queue, borrow/release in try/finally, and reset state. Do not pool cheap objects; use HikariCP rather than your own in production.
  • Dependency injection: receive collaborators via the constructor; wire them at one composition root; containers automate it. It is the clean replacement for Singleton and hard-coded new.
  • Avoid Service Locator, giant constructors and an interface per class.
  • Every creational pattern is justified only by a real variation, cost or test need; say which in the interview.

questions.promptHtml: What is the Prototype pattern and when does copying an object beat constructing a new one?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates the pattern from Java's clone() and checks that you measure cost before choosing it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Prototype creates new objects by copying a configured existing one. It pays off when construction is expensive (parsing, I/O, a large graph) or when I want many variations of a template. I share the immutable heavy parts and copy only the mutable state. If new is cheap, copying is just extra complexity.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Example: spawning 5,000 enemies, each needing a 3 MB mesh and a 40 ms stats parse. Rebuilding is 5,000 x 40 ms = 200 s. Load one prototype, share the immutable mesh, copy hp and position: microseconds each.

Registry["goblin"] -> Enemy prototype (shared Mesh, own hp/pos)
spawn("goblin") -> copy(): new Enemy(sameMesh, hp, new Vec(pos))

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
Enemy copy() { return new Enemy(mesh, hp, new Vec(pos.x, pos.y)); }   // mesh shared, pos copied
fun copy() = Enemy(mesh, hp, pos.copy())   // pos is a data class

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Equating Prototype with Object.clone().
  • Copying an object that holds unique identity or a resource (ID, socket, lock).
  • Using it where construction is already cheap.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Prototype vs flyweight? -> Flyweight shares the heavy immutable part; Prototype creates independent copies; they combine.
  2. How does Spring's prototype scope relate? -> New bean instance per request for the bean; same spirit, different mechanism.
  3. How do you stop aliasing bugs? -> Immutable parts plus explicit copy of mutable ones.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "you call clone()". Senior: when it is not worth it, what is shared vs copied, and the identity problem.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A document editor duplicated styled shapes by re-parsing the template each time; switching to a copy cut a bulk paste of 2,000 shapes from seconds to milliseconds (illustrative).

questions.promptHtml: What is an Object Pool, and what are the rules for using one correctly?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Pools appear in every backend (DB connections, threads). The signal is knowing borrow/release discipline and bounds.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An Object Pool keeps ready-made reusable objects and lends them out instead of creating and destroying them per use. It is worth it for expensive or scarce resources: DB connections, threads, big buffers. Rules: bound the size, always release in finally, reset state on release, and validate or expire stale objects.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A Postgres connection takes roughly 20 to 50 ms to open. At 800 requests/s, opening one per request would burn 16 to 40 seconds of connect time every second. A pool of 20 serves the load with near-zero setup. The fixed maximum gives natural back-pressure: when empty, callers wait with a timeout instead of overwhelming the database.

borrow(timeout) -> use -> release()
active == max and idle == 0  => callers queue, then time out

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Connection c = pool.borrow(500);
try { run(c); } finally { pool.release(c); }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Release not in finally: a leak that slowly drains the pool.
  • Unbounded pool: memory leak in disguise.
  • Handing back a dirty object (open transaction, leftover buffer contents).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is a typical pool library? -> HikariCP for JDBC; do not hand-roll in production.
  2. Pool size rule of thumb? -> Small: about cores * 2 + spindles as a start; measure.
  3. What if the server closed an idle connection? -> Validate on borrow or use maxLifetime shorter than the server timeout.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "it reuses objects". Senior: bounds, back-pressure, state reset, staleness, and sizing against the database, not the app.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: "Connection is not available, request timed out after 30000ms" is the classic symptom of a leak or a pool smaller than concurrency.

questions.contextHtml:
A "duplicate report" feature lets users clone a report template and edit rows. Support tickets: "editing my copy changes the original". The code:

class Report implements Cloneable {
    String name; List<String> rows = new ArrayList<>();
    @Override public Report clone() {
        try { return (Report) super.clone(); }
        catch (CloneNotSupportedException e) { throw new AssertionError(e); }
    }
}
Report copy = original.clone();
copy.rows.add("Q4 total");

After the call, original.rows.size() is 1 larger.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the bug and fix it. How would you test it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "clone() is broken, use serialization everywhere", or just copies the list without explaining why.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are rows mutable strings or objects? Is Report used across threads? Are there other mutable fields?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable the duplicate button or hotfix by copying the list.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Object.clone() is shallow: both reports point to one ArrayList; (b) shared elements if rows are mutable objects; (c) a UI caching bug (red herring: reproduced in a unit test).
  4. How I'd verify each: Unit test comparing copy.rows == original.rows by reference; System.identityHashCode on both lists.
  5. Root cause: Shallow copy of a mutable collection.
  6. Fix: Copy constructor with a deep copy of mutable parts, or immutable lists.
Languages: Java · Kotlin
Report(Report o) { this.name = o.name; this.rows = new ArrayList<>(o.rows); }
Report copy() { return new Report(this); }
data class Report(val name: String, val rows: List<String>)
val b = a.copy(rows = a.rows + "Q4 total")   // immutable lists: sharing is safe
  1. Prevention: Test: mutate the copy, assert the original is unchanged. Prefer immutable collections so sharing is harmless.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not Java serialization in a hot path (microseconds become milliseconds); not JSON round trips that lose types.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Rows are mutable Row objects? -> Copy each row too (true deep copy).
  • Does ArrayList.clone() fix it? -> No, it copies the array but shares the elements.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team shipped a "copy project" feature with a shared config map; one customer's edits changed 40 other projects before it was caught.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: cannot explain shallow vs deep.
  • Hire: identifies the shared list and fixes it with a copy constructor.
  • Strong hire: also covers element mutability, immutability, and a regression test.

questions.contextHtml:
An order API runs 6 pods, HikariCP maximumPoolSize=10 each. At 21:05 latency goes from 80 ms to 30 s and errors show:

HikariPool-1 - Connection is not available, request timed out after 30000ms.
HikariPool stats: total=10 active=10 idle=0 waiting=87

DB CPU is 12%, Postgres pg_stat_activity shows 10 per pod, many in idle in transaction. A deploy shipped at 21:00 with a new refundOrder method. Traffic is normal at 450 req/s.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the pool size to 100." That raises DB load and does not touch the leak.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did the problem start with the 21:00 deploy? Are the active connections moving or stuck? Any long transactions or slow queries?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back the 21:00 deploy; restart pods only if rollback is not enough.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) a connection leak: a code path acquires and never releases (the new method); (b) a transaction held open during a slow external call; (c) real load growth (red herring, traffic is normal); (d) DB slowness (red herring, CPU 12%).
  4. How I'd verify each: select pid, state, now()-xact_start, query from pg_stat_activity where state='idle in transaction'; enable Hikari leakDetectionThreshold=20000 to log the acquiring stack trace; thread dump to see threads blocked in getConnection.
  5. Root cause: refundOrder returns early on a validation failure without closing the connection or committing (release not in finally).
  6. Fix: Short-term rollback. Long-term, always use try-with-resources.
Languages: Java · Kotlin
try (Connection c = ds.getConnection()) {
    if (!valid(o)) return;      // closes via try-with-resources
    refund(c, o);
}
ds.connection.use { c -> if (!valid(o)) return; refund(c, o) }
  1. Prevention: Leak detection in staging, an alert on waiting > 0 for 1 minute and on active == max, code review rule: no manual getConnection without try-with-resources.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not raise the pool size: 6 pods x 100 connections would hit Postgres limits and hide the leak.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Leak is not code but a slow external call inside a transaction? -> Move the call outside the transaction.
  • Why is DB CPU low? -> Connections are idle, not busy: the signature of a leak.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite incident: a rarely used error branch leaked one connection per failure; the pool drained in 11 minutes during a partner outage.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: increases pool size.
  • Hire: finds the leak via stats and pg_stat_activity, fixes with try-with-resources.
  • Strong hire: leak detection, alerts, rollback first, and explains why more connections hurt.

questions.promptHtml: What is dependency injection, how is it different from a DI container and from a Service Locator, and which injection style do you prefer?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: These terms are constantly confused; a senior must explain why hidden dependencies hurt.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: DI means an object receives its collaborators from outside instead of creating or looking them up. A container such as Spring or Dagger is a tool that automates the wiring; DI works without it. A Service Locator, where a class calls Container.get(X.class) inside methods, hides dependencies and is not DI. I prefer constructor injection: the object is valid when built and fields can be final.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Forms: constructor (required deps), setter/property (optional deps), method injection (rare). The composition root, such as main, is the only place that wires the object graph.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
class OrderService {
    private final PaymentGateway gw;
    OrderService(PaymentGateway gw) { this.gw = gw; }     // visible dependency
}
// root: new OrderService(new StripeGateway(System.getenv("STRIPE_KEY")));
// test: new OrderService(o -> { /* record */ });
class OrderService(private val gw: PaymentGateway)
// Hilt: class OrderService @Inject constructor(private val gw: PaymentGateway)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Equating DI with Spring.
  • Container.get(X.class) inside a method: Service Locator through the back door.
  • Nine constructor parameters answered by switching to field injection instead of splitting the class.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not field injection? -> Cannot construct the object in a plain test without reflection; fields cannot be final.
  2. Dagger vs Spring? -> Dagger generates code at compile time (errors early, fast start); Spring wires via reflection at start-up (flexible, runtime errors).
  3. How does DI relate to Singleton? -> The container's singleton scope gives one instance without static access.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "Spring does it with @Autowired". Senior: separates technique from tool, explains hidden deps and testing.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team moved to constructor injection and found two services with a hidden circular dependency that field injection had masked.

questions.contextHtml:
OrderService is untestable: every test hits Stripe's sandbox, takes 1.4 s, and fails when the network is down. A live key is in source control.

class OrderService {
    private final PaymentGateway gw = new StripeGateway("sk_live_...");
    private final Clock clock = Clock.systemUTC();
    void place(Order o) { if (o.createdAt().isBefore(Instant.now(clock).minusSeconds(900))) throw new ExpiredException(); gw.charge(o); }
}

You have 1 day. 300 unit tests will use this class.
questions.promptHtml: How do you make it testable, and what do the tests look like?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use Mockito's @InjectMocks or PowerMock to replace the new." It treats the symptom and leaves the hard-coded secret and clock.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Where else is StripeGateway constructed? Who rotates the key? Does any caller rely on the default constructor?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Rotate the committed live key today; that is a separate security task.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the class creates its own collaborators; (b) the clock is hidden state; (c) no interface boundary for the gateway.
  4. How I'd verify each: Grep new StripeGateway; try writing one test: it cannot avoid the network.
  5. Root cause: Construction is coupled to use.
  6. Fix: Constructor injection of the gateway and clock; wire in the composition root.
Languages: Java · Kotlin
class OrderService {
    private final PaymentGateway gw; private final Clock clock;
    OrderService(PaymentGateway gw, Clock clock) { this.gw = gw; this.clock = clock; }
}
// test
var clock = Clock.fixed(Instant.parse("2026-01-01T10:00:00Z"), ZoneOffset.UTC);
var gw = new FakeGateway();
new OrderService(gw, clock).place(orderCreatedAt("2026-01-01T09:50:00Z"));
assertEquals(1, gw.charges());
class OrderService(private val gw: PaymentGateway, private val clock: Clock)
  1. Prevention: Secrets from env/secret manager; a rule that classes do not call new on collaborators; fakes over deep mocks.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not introduce a DI container for this; manual constructor injection is enough, and I would not mock Clock statics.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Fake or mock? -> A hand-written fake for stateful behavior; a mock when verifying one interaction.
  • How many tests drop in time? -> 300 x 1.4 s = 7 minutes to milliseconds.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team's suite took 25 minutes because of live sandbox calls; after DI and fakes it ran in 40 seconds.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: PowerMock/hacks.
  • Hire: constructor injection and a fake gateway.
  • Strong hire: injects the clock, deals with the leaked key, and shows the composition root.

questions.contextHtml:
A PR introduces a StringBuilderPool and a RequestDtoPool (DTOs of 5 small fields) "to reduce GC". The service handles 3,000 req/s, GC logs show young collections every 2 s taking 4 ms, and p99 latency is 60 ms dominated by DB calls. The author has no benchmark.

RequestDto dto = dtoPool.borrow();
try { fill(dto); handle(dto); } finally { dto.clear(); dtoPool.release(dto); }
questions.promptHtml: What is your review decision and reasoning?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Approves because less allocation sounds faster.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Was GC identified as a bottleneck (pause time, allocation rate)? Do the DTOs cross threads or async boundaries? Is there a benchmark?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Block the merge; no production risk yet.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) allocation of tiny short-lived objects is nearly free in the young generation; (b) the pool adds contention and bug risk; (c) pooled objects living long get promoted to old gen, making GC worse.
  4. How I'd verify each: JMH benchmark with and without the pool; GC logs (-Xlog:gc), allocation profiler (JFR) to see top allocators.
  5. Root cause: Optimization without a measured problem.
  6. Fix: Reject the pools. If GC truly matters, find the real allocation hotspot with JFR.
  7. Prevention: Team rule: performance changes need a measurement in the PR.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would still approve pooling of expensive or scarce resources (connections, Netty direct buffers).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The dto is handed to an async callback after release? -> Use-after-release bug: another request sees its data.
  • When would pooling DTOs be valid? -> Hot path with measured GC pause problems and no alternative; rare in business code.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite service pooled small objects, hit a use-after-release bug, and mixed one user's data into another's response.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: approves.
  • Hire: rejects for no measurement and cheap allocation.
  • Strong hire: names JMH/JFR, use-after-release risk, and where pooling is valid.

questions.contextHtml:
A "duplicate product" feature copies a Product prototype. Afterwards the catalog shows two rows with the same SKU, and inventory updates apply to both. A DBA reports a unique index violation only on one path.

class Product {
    final String id; String sku; List<Image> images; Lock lock = new ReentrantLock();
    Product copy() { return new Product(id, sku, images, lock); }
}
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong with copy()? How would you correct it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make it a deep copy" without distinguishing identity, shared state and resources.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the copy supposed to be: a new entity or a snapshot? Which fields are identity? Are images immutable?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable duplicate; fix the duplicated SKU rows.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) id and sku copied: two entities with the same identity; (b) images shared, so edits alias; (c) the Lock is shared, so unrelated products block each other.
  4. How I'd verify each: Unit test: copy().id != original.id; identity comparison on images and lock.
  5. Root cause: Copying identity and resources, which should be unique per object.
  6. Fix: New identity; deep copy mutable parts; new lock.
Languages: Java · Kotlin
Product copy() { return new Product(IdGen.next(), sku + "-copy", List.copyOf(images), new ReentrantLock()); }
fun copy() = Product(IdGen.next(), "$sku-copy", images.toList(), ReentrantLock())
  1. Prevention: A copy test that asserts identity and resource fields differ.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use clone(); it skips constructors and cannot reassign final fields.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Should the SKU be copied? -> A business rule: SKUs are unique, so generate or require a new one.
  • Are images shared safely? -> If immutable, yes.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite incident: a copied order carried the same payment token and was charged twice.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: only "deep copy".
  • Hire: spots duplicate identity and shared lock.
  • Strong hire: separates identity, shared immutable data and resources, and tests it.

questions.promptHtml: Why do many Java engineers avoid Object.clone(), and what do you use instead? How does the answer change for immutable objects and Kotlin data classes?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests Effective Java depth and the habit of making sharing safe by immutability.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Object.clone() skips constructors, copies shallowly, cannot reassign final fields, and relies on a Cloneable marker with no method, so the contract is vague and bug-prone. I use a copy constructor or copy factory for mutable objects, and for immutable objects I do not copy at all: sharing is safe. In Kotlin copy() on a data class is shallow, fine when the nested parts are immutable.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
clone() bypasses invariants set in constructors and requires every class in the hierarchy to cooperate through super.clone(). Arrays are the only place clone is idiomatic. A copy constructor is explicit about what is copied deeply.

Approach Cost Risk
clone() cheap shallow, skips constructors
copy constructor cheap you must remember each field
serialize/deserialize slow (ms) needs Serializable, loses transient
immutable object none none, if all nested parts immutable

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
Report(Report o) { this.name = o.name; this.rows = new ArrayList<>(o.rows); }
val b = a.copy(rows = a.rows.toList())

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing ArrayList.clone() deep copies elements.
  • Copying objects with mutable elements and calling it deep.
  • Serialization for copying in a hot loop.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When is clone() fine? -> Arrays; or a final class with only immutable fields.
  2. How do records help? -> Immutable value objects need no copy; compact constructors validate.
  3. Cycles in the graph? -> Copy needs a visited map; often a sign to redesign.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "clone is shallow". Senior: why the contract is flawed, choose immutability first, copy only mutable parts.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An aliasing bug from a shallow copy() of a config map corrupted other tenants' settings until sharing was replaced by immutable maps.

questions.contextHtml: Black Friday is 10x normal: 450 req/s becomes 4,500 req/s. Each request holds a connection for about 15 ms. You run 12 pods, maximumPoolSize=10. A teammate proposes maximumPoolSize=200 per pod because "10x traffic". Postgres is max_connections=500 on 8 vCPUs; pg_stat_activity currently shows 120 connections.
questions.promptHtml: What pool configuration do you propose? Show the math.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Multiplies by 10 and approves 200 per pod: 12 x 200 = 2,400 connections against a 500 limit.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Peak concurrency per pod? Slow queries? Are other services on the same DB? Is a pooler like PgBouncer available?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Keep the pool bounded; do not exceed DB capacity.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) concurrency needed is small; (b) too many connections cause DB context switching; (c) pods autoscaling multiplies connections.
  4. How I'd verify each: Little's law: concurrent connections = arrival rate x hold time = 4,500 x 0.015 = about 68 in total, about 6 per pod across 12 pods. Add headroom for spikes: 10 per pod is already enough on average. Check p99 hold time and queue waits in Hikari metrics.
  5. Root cause of the proposal: Sizing from traffic multiples instead of concurrency.
  6. Fix: Keep around 10 to 15 per pod (120 to 180 total), set connectionTimeout small (say 2 s) for fail-fast, cap pod autoscaling by pods x pool <= 0.7 x max_connections (verify with the DB's actual limit and reserved connections). If more pods are needed, add PgBouncer.
  7. Prevention: Load test with realistic hold times; alert on pool wait time.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No 200 per pod: 8 vCPUs cannot execute 2,400 concurrent queries; it increases context switching and latency.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Hold time grows to 100 ms under load? -> 4,500 x 0.1 = 450 connections needed: the real fix is the slow query, not the pool.
  • Autoscaler doubles pods? -> The connection total doubles; set pool per pod from the DB budget.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team scaled pods from 10 to 60 and took the DB down with connection exhaustion, not with CPU.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: 200 per pod.
  • Hire: Little's law and DB limit.
  • Strong hire: ties pods x pool to max_connections, discusses hold time and PgBouncer.

questions.contextHtml:
A homegrown Pool<Connection> is used by a batch service. Two symptoms: (1) intermittent Connection reset errors after quiet nights, first request of the morning fails; (2) some queries run with READ ONLY mode set by a previous borrower, so writes fail with cannot execute INSERT in a read-only transaction. Logs excerpt:

05:58:01 WARN  borrow -> conn#7 used 11h ago
05:58:01 ERROR org.postgresql.util.PSQLException: An I/O error occurred while sending to the backend. (Connection reset)
09:14:22 ERROR cannot execute INSERT in a read-only transaction (conn#3)

The DB's idle timeout is 8 hours; a firewall drops idle TCP after 1 hour.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a retry." That hides both root causes.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Why not HikariCP? Who sets read-only? Do failures occur only after idle gaps? Is there a firewall idle limit?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restart the service before the morning batch; retry the first operation for the stale case.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) stale connections killed by firewall/DB idle timeout, no validation on borrow; (b) state not reset on release (setReadOnly(true) leaks); (c) the DB is flaky (red herring: the timing matches idle gaps).
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare failure times with idle durations in logs (11 h idle > 1 h firewall limit); check which code path sets read-only and whether release resets.
  5. Root cause: The pool treats the connection as a plain object: no liveness check, no state reset.
  6. Fix: Use HikariCP with maxLifetime below the shortest idle limit (for example 30 minutes), keepalive, and reset state.
Languages: Java · Kotlin
void release(Connection c) {
    try { c.rollback(); c.setReadOnly(false); c.setAutoCommit(true); idle.offer(c); }
    catch (SQLException e) { closeQuietly(c); }   // discard if reset fails
}
fun release(c: Connection) {
    try { c.rollback(); c.isReadOnly = false; c.autoCommit = true; idle.offer(c) }
    catch (e: SQLException) { c.close() }
}
  1. Prevention: Test: borrow, change state, release, borrow, assert defaults. Alert on validation failures.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not rely on retries alone, and I would not keep a custom pool when a battle-tested one exists.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Validate on every borrow? -> Cost of a ping; use a cheap isValid(1) or validate only after an idle threshold.
  • Pool behind PgBouncer? -> Transaction pooling changes session state rules; verify.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team spent a week blaming the database for a "first request fails" bug that was a firewall dropping idle connections.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: retry.
  • Hire: stale connections and state reset.
  • Strong hire: maxLifetime below firewall idle limit, discard-on-failed-reset, and tests.

questions.contextHtml:
CheckoutService has this constructor, and a new requirement arrives: pick SMS or email per request based on user preference.

CheckoutService(PaymentGateway g, TaxCalc t, Inventory i, SmsNotifier s, EmailNotifier e,
                Analytics a, AuditLog l, Clock c, Coupons cp) {...}

A dev suggests injecting the whole Spring ApplicationContext and calling ctx.getBean(...) per request. Another suggests field injection to "shorten" the constructor.
questions.promptHtml: What do you do about the constructor, the per-request notifier choice and the two suggestions?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Takes the ApplicationContext idea: it removes the constructor parameters at the cost of hidden dependencies.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does the class do beyond checkout? How many channels will exist? Is choice per user or per event type?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) nine dependencies signal too many responsibilities; (b) per-request choice needs a factory or registry; (c) the context injection is a Service Locator.
  4. How I'd verify each: Group the methods by dependency: pricing (tax, coupons), fulfilment (inventory), notification (sms, email, analytics, audit).
  5. Root cause: A god-service, not a DI problem.
  6. Fix: Split into PricingService, FulfilmentService, and OrderEvents (notification, analytics, audit). Inject a NotifierFactory that picks the channel per request.
Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface NotifierFactory { Notifier forUser(User u); }
class ChannelNotifierFactory implements NotifierFactory {
    private final Map<Channel, Notifier> byChannel;
    public Notifier forUser(User u) { return byChannel.get(u.preferredChannel()); }
}
class ChannelNotifierFactory(private val byChannel: Map<Channel, Notifier>) : NotifierFactory {
    override fun forUser(u: User) = byChannel.getValue(u.preferredChannel)
}
  1. Prevention: Constructor over 5 parameters triggers a design review; no ApplicationContext in business classes.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No field injection (cannot construct in tests without reflection) and no service locator (hides dependencies).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Adding a push channel? -> Register one more Notifier in the map; nothing else changes.
  • Is the factory a singleton? -> Yes, it is in the container; it returns shared stateless notifiers.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite codebase with getBean calls had circular dependencies found only at runtime during a rare code path.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: accepts the locator or field injection.
  • Hire: splits the class and injects a factory.
  • Strong hire: ties the factory into DI scopes, rejects the locator with reasons, adds the extension story.
